summary: We built an interactive tool that finds places on Earth whose terrain matches NASA’s Artemis III candidate landing regions near the lunar south pole. For each region, it compares five terrain measures at the same 100 m scale on both bodies (mean slope, 90th-percentile slope, roughness, relief, and shape) using NASA LRO LOLA elevation data for the Moon and NASA SRTM and ASTER elevation data for Earth. It then ranks bare-ground Earth sites with a % match. Users pick a region on a map of the south pole, see its best Earth analogs with satellite imagery and a feature-by-feature comparison, and check how much sunlight the region receives from NASA’s LOLA illumination maps. They can then drive a rover across the Earth site and switch to the Moon site it stands in for. These accessible locations give mission teams places to test rovers, equipment, and operations before going to the Moon. Earth can’t reproduce lunar gravity, vacuum, or the Sun hanging near the horizon, but showing where the terrain matches, and where it doesn’t, can guide testing and mission planning.
details:
Our app searches for Earth terrain patches that resemble candidate landing regions near the lunar south pole. It compares terrain measurements, ranks the closest matches, and lets users run an interactive rover simulation across the selected terrain. A toggle switches the simulation between the lunar site and its Earth analog, making it easy to compare how the rover encounters similar terrain in both environments and where the analogy has limits.

Earth analogs offer accessible places to test rover operations and NASA equipment without traveling to the Moon. By helping teams investigate terrain challenges on Earth, the project aims to support future research into Earth–Moon analogs and improve equipment and operations for lunar exploration.

The project uses JavaScript, HTML, and CSS for the interactive frontend, with a Python backend built using FastAPI and NumPy. It uses Globe.gl and Three.js for the 3D lunar globe and Leaflet for maps. Earth terrain analysis uses Google Earth Engine with Copernicus GLO-30 elevation and ESA WorldCover data; lunar terrain measurements use LOLA elevation data. The globe uses visualizations derived from NASA LRO/LROC and LOLA data.

The project’s creativity comes from combining terrain matching with interactive graphics. Users can explore lunar candidate regions, compare ranked Earth matches, and switch between Earth and Moon views in the rover simulation. The matching considers mean and 90th-percentile slope, surface roughness, elevation relief, bare-ground coverage, and snow or ice coverage, with a focus on conditions relevant to landing, rover traversal, and robotic operations. The comparison also accounts for important limits: Earth and the Moon differ in gravity, atmosphere, erosion, temperature, and polar illumination. Available dust data differ as well: the Earth data cover airborne dust, while the lunar data describe soil dust. These differences affect how closely an Earth location can represent a lunar environment.
dataRefs: LRO Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) archive
